identification.summary: Russian state cyber-espionage actor that Microsoft tracks as Secret Blizzard and other vendors track as Turla, Snake, Uroburos, Venomous Bear and Waterbug [S1][S2][S4]. Microsoft says it seeks long-term access to systems for intelligence collection, generally looking for information of political importance, and it targets foreign affairs ministries, embassies, government offices and defense organizations worldwide [S2]. It regularly takes over the tools and infrastructure of other threat actors; Microsoft counts at least six such actors over seven years [S2]. Its flagship Kazuar backdoor has grown into a modular peer-to-peer botnet [S4]. In 2025 Microsoft confirmed for the first time that it can operate adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) attacks at the internet service provider (ISP) level inside Russia [S1].
identification.firstObserved: ESET describes Turla as operating since at least 2004 [S5]. The French C4 says it has observed Turla targeting France since 2010 [S7].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Secret Blizzard. Microsoft lists the overlapping names VENOMOUS BEAR, Uroburos, Snake, Blue Python, Turla, Wraith, ATG26 and Waterbug [S1]. MITRE tracks the group as Turla (G0010). 'Snake' names both the actor (in some vendor reporting) and its long-running implant, which the US disrupted in 2023 [S6]. Kaspersky's WhiteBear is described as a parallel project or second stage of its Skipper Turla cluster, with a separate target focus [S9]. Microsoft tracks Storm-0156, Storm-1919 (Amadey), Storm-1837 and Aqua Blizzard as separate actors whose access Secret Blizzard has piggybacked on; they are not aliases [S2][S3][S4].

attribution.sponsor: Russian Federation, Federal Security Service (FSB) Center 16. Microsoft cites CISA's attribution of Secret Blizzard to FSB Center 16 [S1][S2][S4], and US court documents in Operation MEDUSA attribute the Snake malware to a unit within FSB Center 16 [S6]. France's Cyber Crisis Coordination Centre (C4) attributes Turla to the FSB's 16th Centre [S7].
attribution.confidence: US government: attribution to FSB Center 16, stated in the 2023 MEDUSA court-authorized operation and the joint advisory, as reported by press [S6]. France: formal national attribution by the C4 on 2026-07-13, issued the same day as a French Foreign Ministry attribution statement and an EU High Representative statement [S7][S8]. Microsoft relies on CISA's attribution rather than stating its own confidence level [S1][S4]. ESET assesses with high confidence that Gamaredon collaborates with Turla [S5].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and joint analysis with Lumen Black Lotus Labs [S2][S3]; FBI technical operation against the Snake peer-to-peer network [S6]; French C4 and Foreign Ministry attribution statements [S7][S8]; ESET telemetry from Ukrainian machines [S5]; Kaspersky reporting on WhiteBear [S9].

objectives: Strategic political and military intelligence collection through long-term, covert access [S2]. Priorities include foreign ministries, embassies and diplomats, including foreign embassies in Moscow [S1][S2]; Ukrainian military devices, including front-line systems [S3]; and government, diplomatic and defense targets in Europe and Central Asia [S4]. US court documents describe the group stealing sensitive documents from hundreds of systems in at least 50 countries [S6].

sectors: Foreign affairs ministries and embassies / diplomatic entities [S1][S2][S9]
Defense and military organizations, including Ukrainian military devices [S2][S3]
Intelligence services (Afghan General Directorate of Intelligence) [S2]
regions: At least 50 countries, including the United States, per US court documents (as reported) [S6]
targeting.notes: Tasking is selective. ESET saw Turla on only seven machines in Ukraine over about 18 months, against much wider Gamaredon compromise [S5]. Microsoft saw a custom survey tool deployed selectively to devices connecting from Starlink IP addresses, which Microsoft describes as a common signature of Ukrainian front-line military devices [S3]. In India, Secret Blizzard mostly harvested data that Storm-0156 had already staged rather than deploying malware directly [S2].

capabilities.summary: Kazuar is a modular peer-to-peer botnet built from Kernel, Bridge and Worker modules. A single elected Kernel leader limits outbound traffic, internal traffic uses Window Messaging, Mailslot and named pipes, and external C2 uses HTTP, WebSockets or Exchange Web Services [S4]. Delivery uses droppers such as Pelmeni, whose payload is often encrypted against the target's hostname [S4]. The group hijacks other actors' access: Storm-0156 C2 servers since November 2022 (using TwoDash, Statuezy, MiniPocket and a TinyTurla fork) [S2], Amadey bots and a Storm-1837 backdoor in Ukraine in 2024 to install Tavdig and KazuarV2 [S3], and Gamaredon tools that launched or installed Kazuar in 2025 [S5]. ApolloShadow malware, delivered through ISP-level AiTM and a captive-portal redirect, installs a trusted root certificate disguised as a Kaspersky installer, enabling TLS stripping; it also creates a local admin account named UpdatusUser [S1]. Microsoft assesses that this AiTM position is likely enabled by lawful-intercept systems, possibly SORM [S1]. The Snake implant ran a covert peer-to-peer network across compromised computers until the FBI disabled it in 2023 [S6]. Earlier operations used hijacked satellite connections and compromised websites for C2 [S9].

campaigns.name: WhiteBear
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky reports that from February to September 2016 WhiteBear targeted embassies and consular operations worldwide, then expanded to defense-related organizations through June 2017; C2 used compromised websites and hijacked satellite connections.

campaigns.name: Storm-0156 infrastructure takeover
campaigns.summary: Secret Blizzard begins compromising C2 servers of Pakistan-based Storm-0156, then uses them to reach Afghan government targets and to harvest data on Indian military and defense targets; in August 2024 it uses a CrimsonRAT compromise to run TwoDash in India.

campaigns.name: Operation MEDUSA (Snake disruption)
campaigns.summary: The US Justice Department announces a court-authorized operation in which the FBI used a tool called PERSEUS to make Snake implants disable themselves; the US attributes Snake to FSB Center 16; a Five Eyes joint advisory accompanied it.

campaigns.name: Ukraine: Storm-1837 and Amadey piggybacking
campaigns.summary: Microsoft assesses that Secret Blizzard likely used a Storm-1837 backdoor (January 2024) and Amadey bots (March to April 2024) to deliver Tavdig and then KazuarV2 to Ukrainian military devices.

campaigns.name: Gamaredon and Turla collaboration
campaigns.summary: ESET observes Gamaredon tools restarting Turla's Kazuar v3 in February 2025 and deploying Kazuar v2 installers in April and June 2025 on Ukrainian machines.

campaigns.name: ISP-level AiTM against embassies in Moscow (ApolloShadow)
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observes ISP-level AiTM activity redirecting diplomatic devices in Moscow to ApolloShadow, which installs a root certificate for TLS stripping; Microsoft published the report on 2025-07-31.

campaigns.name: French defense research institute compromise
campaigns.summary: The French Foreign Ministry states that a research institute working on sensitive technologies for the French defense industry was targeted in February 2025 by FSB Center 16, leading to exfiltration of a significant volume of data.

campaigns.name: Kazuar P2P botnet disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft publishes analysis of Kazuar as a modular P2P botnet used against government and diplomatic targets in Europe and Central Asia and against Ukrainian systems previously compromised by Aqua Blizzard.

campaigns.name: French and EU attribution
campaigns.summary: On 2026-07-13 the French C4 attributes Turla activity against French entities since 2010 to FSB Center 16. The French Foreign Ministry and the EU High Representative issued attribution statements the same day; the Foreign Ministry cites targeting of Armed Forces Ministry email accounts since 2017, the French Embassy in Moscow network (2018) and a judicial-sector server (2019).

diamond.adversary: FSB Center 16 operators tracked as Secret Blizzard / Turla [S1][S6][S7].
diamond.capability: Kazuar P2P botnet, Tavdig, TwoDash, Statuezy, MiniPocket, TinyTurla variants, ApolloShadow and the Snake implant; hijacking other actors' footholds; ISP-level AiTM [S1][S2][S3][S4][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Commandeered C2 and footholds belonging to Storm-0156, Amadey (Storm-1919), Storm-1837 and Gamaredon [S2][S3][S5]; Kazuar P2P relays with HTTP, WebSocket and EWS C2 [S4]; Snake's covert P2P network [S6]; ISP-level interception position in Russia [S1]; compromised websites and hijacked satellite links in earlier activity [S9].
diamond.victim: Foreign ministries, embassies and diplomats (including in Moscow), government ministries, defense organizations and defense research, Ukrainian front-line military devices, and Afghan and Indian government and military targets [S1][S2][S3][S7][S8].
diamond.socioPolitical: Russian strategic intelligence requirements on foreign policy, NATO and European governments, and the war in Ukraine [S1][S3][S4][S7].
diamond.technology: Windows endpoints and Exchange Web Services [S4]; TLS trust stores and captive-portal flows on ISP-provided connections [S1]; Starlink-connected field devices [S3].

gaps: Primary US documents (the DOJ MEDUSA announcement and the joint Snake advisory) were not opened; their details come from press coverage [S6]. The advisory identifier AA23-129A and the Ryazan facility detail were not verified.

The French C4 statement and the CERT-FR report (CERTFR-2026-CTI-004/005) could not be fetched; details come from search summaries of the C4 and French Foreign Ministry statements [S7][S8]. Press mentions of a specific FSB unit number (Unit 61240), a twelve-country scope and Polish water and energy sabotage are unverified. The sabotage claims may belong to a different FSB Center 16 activity set or EU statement, so do not attach them to Turla without the primary text.
The ESET Gamaredon x Turla report was not opened; findings come from search summaries of the ESET blog and press release [S5].
How Secret Blizzard gained control of the Storm-1837 backdoor and Amadey bots was still under investigation at the time Microsoft published [S3].
Microsoft's assessment that SORM or lawful-intercept systems enable the ISP-level AiTM is a likelihood judgement, not a confirmed mechanism [S1].
A CrowdStrike report dated July 2026 appeared in aggregator results but was not reviewed.
The Kaspersky WhiteBear URL and content come from the imported actor record; the publication month (2017-08) was not re-verified [S9].
Most aliases in the imported record (e.g., ATK13, ITG12, SIG23, UAC-0003/0024/0144, UNC4210) were not confirmed by the sources gathered here.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (environment): key terrain includes diplomatic and government networks, defense research enclaves, Exchange/EWS services, TLS trust stores, and host-nation ISP links serving deployed or diplomatic personnel, especially inside Russia [S1][S4][S8]. STEP 2 (effects): host-nation telecommunications cannot be trusted; ISP-level AiTM plus a rogue root certificate exposes credentials and tokens in transit [S1]. Footholds left by lower-tier actors (criminal botnets, other APTs) can become entry points for this actor [S2][S3][S5]. STEP 3 (threat model): access is gained by piggybacking on an existing foothold or by AiTM/captive-portal lure, followed by a loader (Tavdig, Pelmeni) and then the Kazuar P2P botnet, with an elected leader keeping C2 traffic low, and selective collection [S1][S3][S4]. STEP 4 (COAs): MLCOA is quiet, long-term collection from a small number of high-value diplomatic, government and defense hosts, plus selective targeting of front-line military devices in Ukraine [S2][S3][S5]. MDCOA is covert interception of coalition planning traffic through compromised ISP or host-nation infrastructure and in-memory implants on mission-relevant networks, giving persistent awareness of intentions during a crisis [S1][S4]. Candidate indicators: unexpected root certificates (including fake Kaspersky-branded installers), a local account named UpdatusUser, captive-portal redirects to unfamiliar domains, internal Mailslot or named-pipe chatter between hosts paired with a single host making outbound HTTP/WebSocket/EWS connections, and Tavdig/Kazuar artifacts on hosts already infected with commodity malware [S1][S3][S4].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat any detection of commodity malware (e.g., Amadey) or another APT's implant on mission or partner networks as a possible Secret Blizzard staging point, and escalate hunting accordingly [S2][S3][S5]. (2) Authorities: the 2023 MEDUSA operation shows US law-enforcement authorities can disrupt this actor's infrastructure [S6]. Coordinate DoD defensive actions with FBI/DOJ and with allied attributions such as France's 2026 statement [S7]. (3) Mission assurance: personnel and devices operating on host-nation networks in Russia or contested regions should tunnel all traffic to trusted networks, as Microsoft recommends, and certificate-store monitoring should be part of baseline hardening [S1]. Starlink-connected tactical devices are a demonstrated reconnaissance filter for this actor [S3]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with State Department and embassy IT, allied CERTs (e.g., CERT-FR), Ukrainian partners and DIB partners, because victims span diplomatic, defense-industrial and coalition military domains [S1][S3][S7][S8].

provenance.importedSummary: As a part of our Kaspersky APT Intelligence Reporting subscription, customers received an update in mid-February 2017 on some interesting APT activity that we called WhiteBear. Much of the contents of that report are reproduced here. WhiteBear is a parallel project or second stage of the Skipper Turla cluster of activity documented in another private intelligence report “Skipper Turla – the White Atlas framework” from mid-2016. Like previous Turla activity, WhiteBear leverages compromised websites and hijacked satellite connections for command and control (C2) infrastructure. As a matter of fact, WhiteBear infrastructure has overlap with other Turla campaigns, like those deploying Kopiluwak, as documented in “KopiLuwak – A New JavaScript Payload from Turla” in December 2016. WhiteBear infected systems maintained a dropper (which was typically signed) as well as a complex malicious platform which was always preceded by WhiteAtlas module deployment attempts. However, despite the similarities to previous Turla campaigns, we believe that WhiteBear is a distinct project with a separate focus. We note that this observation of delineated target focus, tooling, and project context is an interesting one that also can be repeated across broadly labeled Turla and Sofacy activity. From February to September 2016, WhiteBear activity was narrowly focused on embassies and consular operations around the world. All of these early WhiteBear targets were related to embassies and diplomatic/foreign affair organizations. Continued WhiteBear activity later shifted to include defense-related organizations into June 2017. When compared to WhiteAtlas infections, WhiteBear deployments are relatively rare and represent a departure from the broader Skipper Turla target set. Additionally, a comparison of the WhiteAtlas framework to WhiteBear components indicates that the malware is the product of separate development efforts. WhiteBear infections appear to be preceded by a condensed spearphishing dropper, lack Firefox extension installer payloads, and contain several new components signed with a new code signing digital certificate, unlike WhiteAtlas incidents and modules.
